UNIFORM PRUDENT INVESTOR ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust

BACKGROUND INFORMATION — UNIFORM PRUDENT INVESTOR ACT
I, Jordan Alex Lee, am serving, or have been asked to serve, as trustee of The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust, executed March 14, 2020. This information sheet describes California's Uniform Prudent Investor Act (Probate Code §§ 16045-16054), the statutory standard of care that governs how a trustee invests and manages trust assets, including the requirement that individual investment and management decisions be evaluated in the context of the trust portfolio as a whole rather than in isolation. This information sheet is educational only. It does not evaluate, approve, or ratify any specific investment, investment strategy, or asset allocation decision made or proposed for The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust; does not determine whether Jordan Alex Lee has satisfied the prudent investor rule or any other fiduciary duty in connection with The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust; and is not investment advice or legal advice. Preparing, reviewing, or signing this information sheet does not itself satisfy, waive, or discharge any duty Jordan Alex Lee owes as trustee of The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust.

THE PRUDENT INVESTOR STANDARD AND THE PORTFOLIO-AS-A-WHOLE RULE
California has adopted the Uniform Prudent Investor Act as Probate Code §§ 16045-16054. Under this article, except where the trust instrument itself provides otherwise, a trustee who invests and manages trust assets owes a duty to the trust's beneficiaries to comply with the prudent investor rule. The statute defines that rule to require a trustee to invest and manage trust assets as a prudent investor would, by considering the purposes, terms, distribution requirements, and other circumstances of the trust, and to exercise reasonable care, skill, and caution in doing so. Critically, the statute does not permit an individual investment or course of action to be judged on its own: it expressly requires that a trustee's investment and management decisions respecting individual assets and courses of action be evaluated not in isolation, but in the context of the trust portfolio as a whole and as a part of an overall investment strategy having risk and return objectives reasonably suited to the trust. The statute also states directly that a trustee may invest in any kind of property or type of investment, or engage in any course of action or investment strategy, consistent with these standards -- the rule is not a list of approved or forbidden asset classes, but a standard for how investment and management decisions are made and evaluated.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), a trustee who invests and manages trust assets owes a duty to the beneficiaries of the trust to comply with the prudent investor rule."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16046(a) (California Legislative Information text), the trustee's general duty to comply with the prudent investor rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16046.)
  "(a) A trustee shall invest and manage trust assets as a prudent investor would, by considering the purposes, terms, distribution requirements, and other circumstances of the trust. In satisfying this standard, the trustee shall exercise reasonable care, skill, and caution. (b) A trustee’s investment and management decisions respecting individual assets and courses of action must be evaluated not in isolation, but in the context of the trust portfolio as a whole and as a part of an overall investment strategy having risk and return objectives reasonably suited to the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16047(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the prudent investor standard itself and the portfolio-as-a-whole rule for evaluating individual investment decisions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16047.)
  Known gap: This is California's own codification of a model uniform act; other states that have enacted versions of the Uniform Prudent Investor Act may have adopted different or modified text, and this document does not address any other state's version. This document does not determine whether any specific trustee's specific investment or management decisions for a specific trust satisfy the prudent investor rule, whether any specific trust portfolio's risk and return objectives are reasonably suited to that trust, or how a court would evaluate any specific decision in the context of a specific portfolio -- those are fact-specific determinations this document does not resolve. This clause cites Probate Code § 16046(a) and § 16047(a) and (b). The subdivisions of § 16047 -- (a) and (b) -- are not independent of each other, since they come from the same statutory section; § 16046 is a separate section from § 16047. Each section was fetched twice independently from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text (after whitespace normalization) returned both times for both sections.

FACTORS A TRUSTEE MUST CONSIDER UNDER THE PRUDENT INVESTOR RULE
The statute enumerates a specific, non-exclusive list of circumstances that are appropriate to consider in investing and managing trust assets, to the extent relevant to the trust or its beneficiaries: general economic conditions; the possible effect of inflation or deflation; the expected tax consequences of investment decisions or strategies; the role that each investment or course of action plays within the overall trust portfolio; the expected total return from income and the appreciation of capital; other resources of the beneficiaries known to the trustee as determined from information provided by the beneficiaries; needs for liquidity, regularity of income, and preservation or appreciation of capital; and an asset's special relationship or special value, if any, to the purposes of the trust or to one or more of the beneficiaries. The statute separately requires a trustee to make a reasonable effort to ascertain facts relevant to the investment and management of trust assets.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) Among circumstances that are appropriate to consider in investing and managing trust assets are the following, to the extent relevant to the trust or its beneficiaries: (1) General economic conditions. (2) The possible effect of inflation or deflation. (3) The expected tax consequences of investment decisions or strategies. (4) The role that each investment or course of action plays within the overall trust portfolio. (5) The expected total return from income and the appreciation of capital. (6) Other resources of the beneficiaries known to the trustee as determined from information provided by the beneficiaries. (7) Needs for liquidity, regularity of income, and preservation or appreciation of capital. (8) An asset’s special relationship or special value, if any, to the purposes of the trust or to one or more of the beneficiaries. (d) A trustee shall make a reasonable effort to ascertain facts relevant to the investment and management of trust assets."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16047(c)-(d) (California Legislative Information text), the enumerated list of factors appropriate to consider, and the duty to ascertain relevant facts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16047.)
  Known gap: This clause cites Probate Code § 16047(c) and (d); this is the same statutory section cited in the companion authority clause on the core prudent investor standard (§ 16047(a)-(b)), so these citations are not independent of that clause's citation, only of the citations to different sections such as § 16046 and § 16048. Each subdivision was fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times. The statutory list is introduced as circumstances that are appropriate to consider 'to the extent relevant to the trust or its beneficiaries' and is not stated as an exhaustive list -- this document does not determine which of these factors are, in fact, relevant to any specific trust, or how a trustee should weigh them against one another for any specific trust or investment decision.

DUTY TO DIVERSIFY, AND ITS PRUDENT-UNDER-THE-CIRCUMSTANCES EXCEPTION
In making and implementing investment decisions, the statute imposes on a trustee a duty to diversify the investments of the trust -- but this duty is not absolute. The same sentence that states the duty also states its exception: the duty to diversify does not apply where, under the circumstances, it is prudent not to diversify. The statute does not itself enumerate what circumstances make non-diversification prudent; it leaves that determination to be made in light of the facts and circumstances of the particular trust and investment decision, informed by the same considerations set out elsewhere in this article (such as the trust's purposes, distribution requirements, and the beneficiaries' other resources).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In making and implementing investment decisions, the trustee has a duty to diversify the investments of the trust unless, under the circumstances, it is prudent not to do so."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16048 (California Legislative Information text), the duty to diversify trust investments and its prudent-under-the-circumstances exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16048.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on a single sentence within a single statutory section, § 16048; there is no second section to cross-reference for independence, so its independence rests solely on the two separately-conducted fetches of that one section (distinct User-Agent headers, identical text returned both times). This is California's own codification of the Uniform Prudent Investor Act; other states' versions of the uniform act may state the diversification duty or its exception differently, or not at all. This document does not determine whether diversifying, or not diversifying, is in fact prudent for any specific trust's assets under any specific set of circumstances -- the statute commits that determination to case-by-case application, not to a fixed rule this document can state in advance.

THE TRUST INSTRUMENT'S POWER TO EXPAND OR RESTRICT THE STANDARD
The prudent investor rule described in this article is a default rule, not one that necessarily applies unaltered to every trust. The statute expressly permits a trust's settlor to expand or restrict the prudent investor rule by express provisions in the trust instrument, and separately provides that a trustee is not liable to a beneficiary for the trustee's good faith reliance on those express provisions. This means the specific standard of care that applies to investment and management decisions for a given trust can only be determined by reading that trust's own instrument together with this default statutory rule, since the instrument may have broadened, narrowed, or otherwise modified what the statute would otherwise require.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) The settlor may expand or restrict the prudent investor rule by express provisions in the trust instrument. A trustee is not liable to a beneficiary for the trustee’s good faith reliance on these express provisions."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16046(b) (California Legislative Information text), the settlor's power to expand or restrict the prudent investor rule by express trust provisions, and the related good-faith-reliance protection for the trustee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16046.)
  Known gap: This clause cites Probate Code § 16046(b), which is a subdivision of the same section (§ 16046) cited for the general duty-to-comply rule in the companion authority clause on the core prudent investor standard -- these two citations are not independent of each other, though both were separately confirmed against § 16047 and § 16048 in the other clauses. The statute's own text says a settlor may 'expand or restrict' the rule by express trust provisions; it does not use the word 'eliminate,' and this document does not take a position on whether or to what degree a restriction could reduce the rule's practical application to a specific trust, or on what express language would be required to accomplish any particular expansion or restriction -- those are drafting and interpretation questions specific to the trust instrument in question, not resolved by this document. This document also does not determine whether any specific trust instrument in fact contains such express provisions, or what those provisions say.

TIMING OF THE PRUDENT INVESTOR DETERMINATION: NO HINDSIGHT
The statute fixes the vantage point from which compliance with the prudent investor rule is measured: compliance is determined in light of the facts and circumstances existing at the time of a trustee's decision or action, and not by hindsight. Under this rule, a later, unfavorable outcome for a particular investment or course of action does not, by itself, establish that the decision failed to meet the prudent investor standard when it was made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Compliance with the prudent investor rule is determined in light of the facts and circumstances existing at the time of a trustee’s decision or action and not by hindsight."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16051 (California Legislative Information text), compliance with the prudent investor rule is judged at the time of the decision or action, not by hindsight (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16051.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on a single sentence within a single statutory section, § 16051, distinct from the sections cited in the other authority clauses in this set, so its citation is independent of those. Its independence rests on the two separately-conducted fetches of § 16051 itself (distinct User-Agent headers, identical text returned both times). This is California's own codification of the Uniform Prudent Investor Act; other states' versions may state this timing rule differently or not include it. This document does not determine what facts and circumstances existed at the time of any specific trustee's specific decision or action, or whether that decision or action was, in fact, prudent when made -- those are fact-specific determinations this document does not resolve.
